text.p: These are the leading stories in the Pakistani press on Saturday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- President Farooq Leghari said corruption trials would be concluded within two months. He said that if an accused indulges in delaying tactics his property may be confiscated and he may be disqualified from contesting elections or dismissed if he is a government servant until the court reaches a decision.

- At least seven activists of the Moslem militant Sunni Tehrik were arrested after a 25-minute hide-and-seek with the police during a protest against induction of an Ahmadi as a minister in the Sindh provincial government.
- India has ruled out any formal talks with Pakistan during the South Asian regional ministerial conference next week but confirmed there would be contacts between the two sides.

- The International Monetary Fund appears to have delayed the resumption of loans as Pakistan's economic managers reported that the latest bank borrowing figures had upset the calculations of the caretaker government and the IMF officials.
- Several religious parties have called a strike on Saturday in the province of Sindh to protest against the induction of an Ahmadi as a minister in the provincial cabinet.
- The Supreme Court will take up for preliminary hearing the petition of deposed prime minister Benazir Bhutto against dismissal of her government on Saturday.
- Pakistan asked the International Monetary Fund to revive an enhanced structural adjustment facility from January 15.
- A senior U.S. official refused to rule out sanctions against China for "transferring nuclear and military technology to Pakistan", calling the deals "a moving target".
- British Gas and Gaz de France are said to be interested in jointly bidding for state-run Sui Southern Gas Company.

- Forex reserves, excluding gold reserves, rose to $745 million from $715 million while notes in circulation registered an increase of 4.989 billion rupees, according to the State (central) Bank of Pakistan.

- The International Monetary Fund is likely to indicate in the middle of next week a reformulated programme of financing Pakistan's budgetary deficit, Shahid Javed Burki, economic adviser to the prime minister, told reporters in Washington.
- Jamaat-i-Islami leader Qazi Hussain Ahmad said the World Bank had instructed its representatives in the caretaker government to suck out the remaining blood of the nation by imposing new taxes.
